title: Problems of an Economy
tagline: Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost: what, how and for whom — and what every choice gives up.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE Economics syllabus registered in this subject’s baseline (the 2026-27 session syllabus as reproduced by Shaalaa and Jagran Josh; the official cisce.org PDFs were not retrievable). Every question and answer is original practice, no board examination paper was consulted, and no figure is presented as an official statistic.

overview.intro: Every economic system, however rich or planned, faces the same three problems — what to produce, how to produce, for whom to produce — because every system works with limited resources against unlimited wants. This chapter studies those problems as connected parts of one situation rather than as a list. Choice is forced by scarcity; every choice has an opportunity cost, which is the value of the next best alternative given up; and the technique and distribution decisions carry costs of their own. The ideas here — scarcity, choice, opportunity cost and the trade-off made visible — are the analytical core of the whole course, and the exam questions that separate strong candidates from weak ones are almost always questions of cost.

learningOutcomes: Explain how scarcity gives rise to the three basic problems.
Define opportunity cost and identify it in given choices.
Analyse the what-to-produce problem as a choice between goods and services.
Analyse the how-to-produce problem as a choice of technique.
Analyse the for-whom-to-produce problem as a question of distribution.

blocks.text: Scarcity converts desire into decision. When resources were unlimited, every want could simply be satisfied and no question would arise; because they are not, the moment a resource is committed to one use it is unavailable for another — scarce means have alternative uses, which is precisely why that commitment is a choice — and a choice has been made whether or not anyone feels they decided anything. That is the sense in which the three basic problems are forced: they are not optional questions for economists but the standing agenda of every household, firm and government. A family choosing between tuition and a new refrigerator, a firm choosing between two machines, a government choosing between a canal and a power station — each is answering what, how and for whom with the same limited means. Economics supplies the discipline for those decisions: identify the alternatives, name the cost, and compare the benefits.

items: Committing a resource to one use closes its other uses — the choice is made by the commitment itself.
The three problems face every decision-maker: household, firm and government alike.
Better decisions come from naming alternatives explicitly rather than choosing by habit.
Scarcity guarantees the questions never finish; solving one round simply starts the next.

learn.title: Opportunity cost: the price of every choice

blocks.text: The opportunity cost of a decision is the value of the next best alternative that the decision rules out. It is not the sum of everything unchosen — the school wing the district did not build, the road it did not lay and the clinic it did not open are together only what was forgone in total; the opportunity cost is the single best of them, the one that would have been chosen had the first choice not been made. This precision makes the concept usable: a student who gives up an evening of cricket to study has an opportunity cost of one evening’s recreation, not of everything else in the world. Opportunity cost is measured in what is given up, not in the money spent, which is why it applies equally to a household’s time, a firm’s capital and a government’s budget.

items.meaning: The value of the next best alternative sacrificed by a choice.
items.context: Every committed rupee, hour or hectare has an opportunity cost.

items.meaning: The single runner-up use that the choice actually rules out.
items.context: Counting every rejected option overstates the cost; only the runner-up counts.

items.meaning: The exchange implicit in a choice: more of one thing means less of another.
items.context: Trade-offs are visible when the same resource cannot serve two uses at once.

items.meaning: Deciding on a small additional unit rather than an all-or-nothing amount.
items.context: Most economic decisions are marginal: one more hour, one more acre, one more machine.

blocks.text: The what-to-produce problem decides the composition of national output: which goods and how much of each. The decision is a choice between consumer goods and capital goods, between food and factories, between guns and butter — a phrase economics uses because the trade-off is so stark in wartime that everyone can see it. An economy that devotes its land and labour to more food today enjoys fuller tables now and slower industrial growth later; one that devotes them to machines accepts thinner tables now for greater output later. The same logic runs within categories: a hectare growing cotton cannot grow wheat, and a classroom teaching engineering cannot teach medicine at the same hour. In a market economy the composition is settled by what pays; in a planned economy, by what the plan prioritises; in a mixed economy, by both.

blocks.caption: One resource, three competing claims
rows: The schools, and the trained generation they would produce
Wheat for the family and market
The wheat output the same hectare could have yielded
The healthcare the complex’s site could have provided

learn.title: Problems two and three: how to produce, for whom

blocks.text: The how-to-produce problem chooses the technique of production: labour-intensive methods that employ many hands and little machinery, or capital-intensive methods that employ few and produce more per worker. There is no universally correct answer — it depends on what is scarce. Where labour is abundant and capital scarce, as in a populous developing country, labour-intensive technique uses the economy’s plentiful factor and spreads incomes; where labour is skilled and capital cheap, machinery lifts output per head. The for-whom-to-produce problem then divides what has been made. In a market economy, distribution follows the ability to pay, which rewards effort and risk but concentrates shares where income concentrates; in a planned economy, rules distribute more evenly but weaken the link between effort and reward. Every mixed economy argues endlessly about this third question because it is where economics touches family life directly.

items: Labour-intensive technique employs more people at lower output per worker; capital-intensive reverses both.
The correct technique depends on relative scarcity: use the factor the economy has plenty of.
Distribution by ability to pay rewards effort and risk but produces inequality.
Distribution by plan rule flattens inequality but weakens the incentive to produce more.
Mixed economies split the question: markets distribute, the state redistributes.

learn.title: The three problems as one connected decision

blocks.text: The three problems are best understood as one decision seen from three sides. A government deciding on a river project answers what to produce — irrigation infrastructure instead of consumer goods; how to produce — with machines on a large scheme or with local labour on a smaller one; and for whom — the farmers of one valley, or taxpayers at large who financed it. Because the same scarce resources stand behind all three answers, the problems are linked: choosing the project settles the goods not made, the technique not used and the share not distributed, all at once. Opportunity cost is the thread that runs through all three, and a complete economic answer names the cost of each choice. That habit — of asking not only what a decision gains but what it forgoes — is the discipline this chapter exists to install.

items.text: A family spends its annual surplus on a wedding instead of on a shop; the shop’s future income is the opportunity cost of the celebration.
items.note: For whom to produce at family scale: the same income decides which want is served.

items.text: A firm buys a machine that does the work of six workers; output per head rises, six wages stop.
items.note: How to produce: the capital-intensive choice raises productivity and cuts employment together.

figures.caption: Figure: the production trade-off made visible
figures.description: A downward-sloping curve plotted with consumer goods on one axis and capital goods on the other, with three marked points: a point of heavy consumption now, a point of heavy investment now, and a middle point. Arrows along the curve show that moving towards investment moves away from consumption, and the label names the curve as the trade-off every economy faces.

keyPoints: The three basic problems are forced by scarcity; none can be avoided by any economic system.
Committing a resource to one use closes its alternatives — the choice is inherent in the commitment.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative, not the sum of all alternatives forgone.
The what-to-produce problem is a choice about the composition of national output.
The how-to-produce problem is the choice between labour-intensive and capital-intensive technique.
The correct technique depends on relative scarcity of labour and capital in that economy.
The for-whom-to-produce problem decides distribution: by ability to pay, or by plan rules.
The three problems are one decision seen from three sides, linked by the same scarce resources.
Economic discipline means naming the opportunity cost of every choice, not only its benefit.
examFocus: Define opportunity cost precisely — next best alternative — and lose no marks to the word “sum”.
Identify opportunity cost in a given situation by first naming the runner-up.
Analyse what to produce through a specific trade-off, such as food against machinery.
Analyse how to produce by asking which factor is scarce: labour or capital.
Analyse for whom to produce through the distribution mechanisms of market and plan.
Answer long questions with the linked structure: choice made, cost paid, benefit expected.

questions.prompt: The three basic problems of an economy arise because:
options: Resources are limited and wants are unlimited
People disagree about what is fair
questions.answer: Resources are limited and wants are unlimited
questions.explanation: What, how and for whom are all forced by the single condition of scarcity; disagreement about fairness and price fluctuations are real but consequential, not the origin of the problems.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the problems to poverty — rich economies face exactly the same three questions with larger means.

questions.prompt: The opportunity cost of a decision is:
options: The value of the next best alternative given up
The money spent on the decision
Every alternative that was not chosen
questions.answer: The value of the next best alternative given up
questions.explanation: Only the runner-up alternative counts, because that is the one the choice actually displaced. Summing every rejected option overstates the cost, and money spent is a payment, not necessarily the true forgone value.
questions.commonMistake: Adding up all rejected alternatives — opportunity cost counts only the next best one.

questions.prompt: An economy with abundant labour and scarce capital should normally favour:
questions.explanation: The technique should use the factor the economy has plenty of: labour-intensive methods employ the abundant factor, spread incomes and avoid costs on the scarce one. Capital scarcity makes machine-heavy methods expensive relative to the people they replace.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming modern means capital-intensive everywhere — the correct technique depends on local scarcity.

questions.prompt: Which is the clearest example of the what-to-produce problem?
options: A country devoting more land to factories instead of farms
A firm paying higher wages to skilled workers
A family saving part of its income
A bank charging interest on loans
questions.answer: A country devoting more land to factories instead of farms
questions.explanation: The composition of output — industrial goods instead of food — is exactly what to produce. Wage rates are factor pricing, saving is a household decision, and bank interest is the reward of capital.
questions.commonMistake: Mistaking any hard decision for the what-to-produce problem; it must change what the economy makes.

questions.prompt: Complete: the opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the ________ best alternative that is ________ .
questions.explanation: The definition turns on two words: next identifies the single runner-up, and given up records that the cost is what the choice closed off rather than what it spent.
questions.commonMistake: Writing “all alternatives” instead of “next best”, which turns the cost of one choice into the total of everything unchosen.

questions.prompt: Define opportunity cost and identify it in this choice: a student spends the evening studying instead of playing cricket.
questions.answer: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative sacrificed by a choice. Here the student chose studying over cricket, so the opportunity cost of the study evening is the recreation, rest and practice it displaced — the cricket match that would have been the next best use of those hours. Money is not involved: the cost is measured in the forgone alternative, not in spending.
questions.explanation: The definition earns one mark and the identification the rest, and the closing sentence shows the concept is understood as forgone value rather than expenditure.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the cost as “time wasted on study”, which reverses the direction of the sacrifice.

questions.prompt: Explain the for whom to produce problem and how a mixed economy approaches it.
questions.answer: The for whom to produce problem decides how the nation’s output is shared: who receives the staples and who receives the finer goods, and in what quantities. In a market economy the question answers itself through the ability to pay, so shares follow income, which rewards effort and risk but concentrates output where income concentrates. A mixed economy accepts market distribution as the base because it preserves incentives, and then corrects its extremes through taxation and public services — schools, health care, subsidised food and rural employment — so that basic wants are met even where ability to pay is low. The recurring political argument in a mixed economy is exactly where that correction should stop.
questions.explanation: The question wants the mechanism and the mixed-economy response together: distribution by ability to pay, tempered by redistribution, with the incentive logic stated rather than assumed.
questions.commonMistake: Answering only that the rich get more, without naming the mechanism or the correction mixed economies apply.

questions.prompt: Explain the how to produce problem, and why the answer differs between a populous developing country and an industrialised one.
questions.answer: The how to produce problem chooses the technique of production: labour-intensive methods that employ many workers with simple tools, or capital-intensive methods that employ few workers with machinery and produce more per head. The choice is not a matter of taste but of relative scarcity. In a populous developing country labour is abundant and capital is scarce, so labour-intensive technique uses the plentiful factor, keeps wages flowing to many households and avoids interest costs on borrowed machines — a road built with pickaxes and shovels may cost more per kilometre in effort yet leave more income in the village. In an industrialised country labour is scarce and expensive while capital is plentiful and cheap, so machinery that replaces ten workers per machine raises output per head, keeps prices low and still leaves workers for the services machines cannot do. The technique that is correct in one economy is wasteful in the other, and mixing them carelessly either wastes scarce capital or wastes abundant labour.
questions.explanation: The problem must be defined as a technique choice, and the two economies explained through the scarcity of their factors rather than through wealth as such. The concluding sentence — that the wrong choice wastes whichever factor is scarce — shows the principle is general.
questions.commonMistake: Saying rich countries should use machines and poor countries should not, without linking the technique to relative factor scarcity.

questions.prompt: A farmer has one hectare and must choose between cotton for the mill and wheat for the market. Analyse the decision under all three basic problems, identifying the opportunity cost in each.
questions.answer: What to produce: the hectare can serve only one crop, so the choice determines the composition of the farm’s output — fibre for industry or food for the market. If cotton is chosen, the opportunity cost is the wheat yield the same hectare could have produced, valued at the market price the wheat would have fetched. How to produce: each crop implies its own technique — cotton’s plucking seasons and pesticide schedule against wheat’s sowing and irrigation rhythm — using the same family labour differently and the same scarce water in different quantities. Choosing cotton’s technique costs the water and labour pattern wheat would have required, and that is this problem’s opportunity cost. For whom to produce: cotton income arrives when the mill buys and is shared with the hired labour and the moneylender to whom input credit is owed; wheat income arrives at harvest and feeds the household first, with surplus sold. Choosing cotton therefore forgoes a direct food supply for the family and replaces it with cash income — the distribution effect is the third cost. The decision is thus one choice wearing three faces, and a farmer who weighs only the cash price of cotton is weighing one face while the other two quietly decide the outcome.
questions.explanation: The answer must walk all three problems in order and identify a distinct opportunity cost in each — yield, technique, distribution — because the question explicitly asks for cost under every head. The closing line makes the analytical point: single-face weighing is how bad economic decisions are made.
questions.commonMistake: Analysing only what to produce and stopping, treating how and for whom as consequences rather than as problems with costs of their own.

questions.prompt: “Every solution to an economic problem creates the next problem.” Explain this statement with reference to opportunity cost and the three basic questions.
questions.answer: The statement captures the arithmetic of scarcity. When an economy solves what to produce by building a steel plant, the land, labour and capital committed are no longer available for the schools, hospitals or houses they could have made — the solution has created the next what-to-produce problem, now sharpened by the plant’s success in drawing workers. Solving how to produce with capital-intensive machinery raises output per head but creates the employment question that labour-intensive technique would have avoided, which is a fresh how problem in the domain of jobs. Solving for whom to produce through redistribution lifts basic consumption but changes the incentive to earn the taxed income, opening a new distribution problem between those who pay and those who receive. None of this makes the original decisions wrong — the steel plant may still be the best choice — but it shows why economic problems do not end: each solution reallocates scarcity rather than removing it, and opportunity cost is the ledger that records what the next problem will be made of. That is why economics teaches comparison at the margin rather than the hunt for a costless option.
questions.explanation: The analytical work is to instantiate the claim in all three problems — steel and schools, machines and jobs, taxes and incentives — and then resolve the paradox honestly: problems multiply because solutions reallocate scarcity, not because choices fail. The margin is the correct closing concept.
questions.commonMistake: Answering philosophically without a single worked example from the three problems, which leaves the claim unproved.
